analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 10% through 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card rates at 10% — sponsored by an independent and a Republican with two Democratic cosponsors — has sat untouched in the Senate Banking Committee since February 2025, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a hard ceiling of 10% on credit card interest rates, counting fees toward the cap so lenders can't dodge it. A lender caught knowingly charging more would forfeit all the interest on the debt, and cardholders could sue within two years to get back every interest charge and fee they paid. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the FTC would enforce it under existing consumer credit law, and the whole cap would expire on January 1, 2031.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that carry a credit card balance from month to month. Credit card rates today run far above 10%, so the cap would cut their interest bills sharply, and the private right of action would let borrowers claw back illegal charges. Stronger state rate-cap laws would stay in place.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on credit card borrowing at 10%, including all finance charges, so cardholders carrying a balance pay far less in interest.
Prevents lenders from dodging the cap with add-on fees: any fees that aren't technically finance charges can't be used to evade the limit, and their total can't exceed the finance charges assessed.

Gives borrowers real teeth: a lender that knowingly overcharges forfeits the entire interest on the debt, and the cardholder can sue within two years to recover every interest charge, finance charge, or fee paid.

Makes violations subject to civil liability under the Truth in Lending Act, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Federal Trade Commission, on top of the borrower's own right to sue.
Leaves stronger state consumer protections fully in place rather than overriding them.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies that earn most of their card revenue from interest well above 10%. They would lose that income, and some lenders would likely respond by approving fewer applicants or trimming card perks rather than lend at a rate they can't price for risk.

drawbacks.text: A hard 10% ceiling gives lenders no way to price for risk, so the most likely response is to deny cards or cut credit lines for applicants with poor credit rather than lend at 10% — some of the people the bill aims to help could lose access to credit altogether.
The cap is temporary: it sunsets on January 1, 2031, so any relief would end unless Congress renews it.

The bill caps interest and finance charges but does nothing about the underlying debt itself — borrowers still owe what they borrowed, and fees that fall outside the finance-charge definition are only limited in aggregate, not eliminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households who carry credit card balances at rates far above 10%, this would be one of the largest direct cuts in borrowing costs Congress has considered, and the anti-evasion and forfeiture provisions make it more than symbolic. The honest cost is that lenders who can no longer price risk would likely pull credit from the weakest applicants, so some high-risk borrowers would trade expensive credit for no credit. The sunset in 2031 limits both the help and the harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in February 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act on February 4, 2025, joined from the start by Republican Senator Josh Hawley.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the standard first stop that most bills never get past.

No further action appears in the record: the committee has held no hearing or vote, and the Senate has not taken it up. Three senators total (one Republican, two Democrats) had signed on as cosponsors.
The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically still alive, but bills that sit in committee this long with this little sponsorship rarely move.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers are better off so far: because the bill never advanced, the current system of rates well above 10% remains in place and no interest revenue is at risk.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card interest rates at 10% on February 4, 2025.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced, making it a bipartisan pairing.

for.name: Two Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total Senate support to four members.

against.name: Tim Scott
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee took the bill by referral on February 4, 2025 and has scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote since; nothing beyond the referral appears in the action history.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: The card industry has consistently opposed statutory rate caps of this kind, which would cut off the interest income that is the core of card-issuer profits.

sides.party_line_note: Support is bipartisan but very thin: an independent (Sanders), a Republican (Hawley), and two Democratic cosponsors — 4 of 100 senators — with no recorded opposition votes because the bill never got one.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (card-issuing banks and finance companies)
industries.note: Card APRs commonly run around 20% or higher, and interest is the core of issuer profits from borrowers who carry balances. A 10% all-in cap with an anti-fee-evasion clause and forfeiture of interest for knowing violations would erase most of that revenue and close the usual workaround of piling on fees.

analysis.trajectory: With only four Senate supporters, no committee action in the months since referral, and no sign the Banking Committee will hold a hearing, the most likely path is that the bill sits in committee and dies when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless Sanders uses pressure tactics (such as attempting to force a vote by unanimous consent) that so far have not appeared in the record.
